description:
I'm developing SECOND CHANCE, a pixel-art lunar engineering mystery game for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players explore a Moon base, investigate electrical failures, analyze NASA-derived data, and rewind decisions to discover what went wrong.

I'm interested in game development, space exploration, engineering, and finding creative ways to make science engaging. Our goal is to build something that's not just educational, but genuinely fun to play.
summary: SECOND CHANCE is a pixel art adventure game that teaches students ages 12–16 how to think like engineers. The primary goal is to solve 3 electrical emergencies, and can rewind their decisions to test alternative paths and outcomes. The game models energy generation, battery storage, and consumption. For one mission, we integrated NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter terrain data with JPL Horizons solar-position calculations to model how lunar terrain affects sunlight availability. SECOND CHANCE addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge making students utilize problem solving skills in space engineering. Students must understand engineering tradeoffs while making hypotheses and testing solutions to problems. Our goal is to allow students to learn and grow from mistakes in a controlled and fun environment.
details: In Second Chance, you play as a junior engineer investigating power failures at a moon base. You’ll interact with elements throughout each level to piece together the cause of the power outage. The key gameplay element in Second Chance is that you can rewind time. So, if you make a bad decision, no worries! You can go back in time and make a different decision to see how your actions affect the outcome. Second Chance is about keeping the lunar base running even without our ever-reliable source of energy: sunlight. The game was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python. AI tools were used to help with the game design process. Our final step involved using NASA’s LOLA terrain data and JPL Horizons Sun-position data to calculate when our location on the Moon would be in sunlight or shadow. Through this, we hope to make engineering fun for students ages 12-16, while showing them the importance of understanding why something works, and not just if it works.
